## Round 1 — Authors' Response

We would like to clarify that the focus of our work is not on the prediction of function. Such prediction tasks (e.g., does this sequence have the expected functionality?) can often be achieved with supervised machine learning methods, such as random forest models successfully used by Groher et al, or deep forward neural networks as in Angenent-Mari et al. In particular, Groher et al also exploit their models to filter the best sequences out of in-lab selection experiments (SELEX or directed evolution), starting from an initial library, and improving the target performances. These models, however, cannot be directly used to generate de novo functional sequences.
In contrast to these works, our RBM is a generative model, capable of sampling new, completely de novo, functional sequences. The RBM is trained on a dataset of natural sequences in an unsupervised fashion. Intuitively, the model learns to extract frequent statistical patterns (at the level of conservation or correlations) that are then combined in non-trivial ways for the generation of novel aptamers. We have then performed high-throughput generation of sequences and SHAPE-driven experimental verification of their functionality.
In addition, we believe it is fair to state that the RNA functionalities considered in the works cited above, such as
(1) Optimizing the P1 stem of tetracycline-aptamers (6-10 nucleotides) starting from a random pool of sequences, to improve the dynamic range in the switching behavior by Goher et al.,
(2) Realizing an one toehold switcher structure, with a stem, a bulge and a loop (12 nucleotides in the toehold and 18 in the stem) by Angenent-Mari et al, with a ~20-40 nt variable region designed from SELEX sequence data,
are somewhat simpler than ours. In our manuscript, we design new RNA sequences coding for two alternative structures (including about 100 nucleotides, 4 helices with a complex pattern of secondary and tertiary contacts) controlled by the presence/absence of a metabolite.
Last of all, in our work, the target structure/function is not unique: we do not constrain the generated sequences to correspond to one particular aptamer structure in the SAM-riboswitch family. We design new sequences that reproduce the variability of structures and functions of natural SAM riboswitches. Not all the aptamers among the natural ones which we have probed are switching (~60% responsive in 150 conclusive tested aptamers ), see also Fig. 5 in the new manuscript showing SHAPE-MaP reactivities on two natural aptamers. We thus expect that in the SAM-riboswitch family each aptamer has a slightly different structure and response to SAM, and that the designed sequences reproduce this rich variability.
We now give a more detailed description of the differences/similarities of our method and the works cited by Reviewer 1:
● Groher et al. 2018.
In this paper a pipeline combining experiments and multiple ML methods (secondary structure predictions, graph modeling, features classification, random forest, convolutional neural networks) is introduced to select good P1-stem (with 8 to 10 nucleotides) candidates to improve the dynamic range (quantitative ratio of the on and off states) for tetracycline aptamers. These models exploit carefully manually chosen features (free energy, GC content, hydrogen bonds, …) on which a model is trained, to predict the aptamer performance and optimize a subset of the sequence (P1 stem).
Our approach differs in several key aspects: (1) our model is trained on sequence data only in an unsupervised fashion: features are thus extracted in an automatic way and not chosen a priori; (2) it is simpler, requiring a single neural network model (RBM) for the generation of novel functional sequences: RBM is a generative model, not a supervised classifier like the neural networks used in the cited work; (3) we tackle the difficult task of de novo designing a complete riboswitch aptamer domain with >100 nts, involving several helices, a pseudoknot, and other structural elements, compared to the single stem (~10 nts) in Groher et al.
● Angenent-Mari et al. 2020.
This work focuses on functional prediction with supervised neural networks, for toeholds having a one stem-loop structure, with an on-off regulatory effect on protein translation, and a total of 75 variable nucleotides in the sequence (see Fig. S1A in the paper). In lab-selection from an initial library of natural sequences is performed, and ML is used to classify sequences and predict on/off dynamical ratio, with predictions validated by experimental scans.
As a summary, the main differences between this work and ours are: (1) SAM riboswitches have more complex and diverse possible structures (with multiple helices and a complex network of secondary & tertiary contacts) than a single hairpin-loop structure, making the design problem harder; (2) we introduce ML methods to design novel sequences, not to classify them.
● Iwano et al. 2022
This paper implements the RaptGen model that focuses on aptamer design in SELEX. These aptamers have much shorter sequences (~30 nts) than the ones considered in our work (~108nts). To answer the Reviewer’s point 1, we have considered below the similar RfamGen model (from Sumi et al. 2023), which, similarly to RaptGen, is a variational autoencoder incorporating a covariance model grammar, and compared with the RBM model on the SAM-I riboswitches studied in our paper.
Please notice that, in a previous work (Di Gioacchino et al. PLOS Comp. Bio. 2021), we have trained an RBM model from SELEX data on small (40 nts) aptamers selected to bind thrombin, with a setting more similar to the works above than the present manuscript.
We agree with Reviewer 1 that the introduction of our manuscript was not properly pointing out the state-of-the-art on the use of machine learning for the prediction of functionality in RNA aptamers and the Discussion Section was not clearly comparing our method with previous works. We have therefore expanded our literature review in the introduction (starting at line 53 of new version) and in the final discussion of our paper (line 676), with an explicit in silico comparison with other ML methods as asked in the point 1 below. Following point 1 of Reviewer 2 we have also extended the computational experiments to other riboswitch families (line 214 of the new version).
1) Conduct an in-silico comparative analysis of their RBM technique with a range of other unsupervised learning architectures (standard and emergent) to demonstrate that this technique is indeed advancing the field of RNA switch design using ML techniques and is not just “another” technique of comparable predictive capacity to others published in the past when used on their particular use case. Furthermore, the authors should generate a baseline for their predictive method through a comparison with the use of traditional non-machine learning energy-based calculations for secondary structure prediction using thermodynamic principles predictive capacity of using traditional energy-based calculations such as through the use of the features automatically provided by software packages like NUPACK and ViennaRNA that can calculate minimum free energy and ensemble defect of RNA sequences.
As emphasized above, we believe our approach is new, as we are not aware of previous works using ML that (1) design RNA sequences able to switch structures with generative models learned from natural riboswitch sequences of the same family only, (2) validate the structural switch by a novel high-throughput experimental SHAPE test of the designed sequences (as kindly noticed by Reviewer 1 in his/her report).
We agree with Reviewer 1 that base-line models are essential for the assessment of performances. In our work, we have used Covariation Models (Infernal) as a base-line framework reproducing only the constraints coming from the secondary structure (with the corresponding 1- and 2-point statistics); we have also considered an unknotted version of CM, which allowed us to include the pseudoknot. As shown in the Table of Fig. 9, we found that only 3 out of 20 sequences designed with denoised CM and 1 out of 16 sequences generated by the unknotted CM could switch. These results confirm that generating functional riboswitches (with reasonable success probability) requires going beyond secondary-structure constraints.
Regarding the comparisons with secondary-structure folding energies: In Fig. 8 (previously numbered as Fig. 7), we compare the RBM sores with the ViennaRNA pairing energies of the P1 helix and the pseudoknot PK for all tested sequences. Interestingly, we find that the sequences able to switch are not the most stable for P1 and Pk, but have intermediate ranges of binding energies, likely to facilitate the switching behavior thanks to a larger flexibility.
Last of all, we compare in the new manuscript our generative model with the recent RfamGen model (from Sumi et al 2023), which like RaptGen, is a variational autoencoder (VAE) using a covariance model grammar for the encoding RNA sequences. In the new Supplementary Materials, we have added Supplementary Section L “Comparison to RfamGen” and Fig. S25 (reproduced below) to compare the generation of SAM-riboswitches by the RFamGen and RBM models. We find that RBM-generated sequences (blue) reproduce the distribution of natural sequences (gray) even according to the assigned by the VAE (panel B) of designed sequences.
This suggests that RfamGen does not distinguish between RBM-generated and natural sequences. On the contrary, RfamGen sequences are shifted to lower RBM scores compared to natural sequences (panel A). Taken together, these results suggest that the scoring function of the RBM model is more accurate than the one of RfamGen.
As a last point we would like to underline that in contrast to VAEs, RBM produces interpretable sequence motifs, informative about key nucleotides and positions for the riboswitch functionality through the position weight matrices (weights of RBM) connecting the sequence and the hidden (latent) units. See Figure 3B and C. In contrast, deep VAEs are far less interpretable.
2) The authors provide a Git with their source code and a Pluto.jl notebook implemented in Julia. This is great, but unfortunately, this choice requires the reader to host their code locally to reproduce the results of this work. I believe this is a big barrier to reproducibility, and the authors should aim to reduce this barrier even through either of the two paths. A) Hosting a live demo of their technique for RNA riboswitch functionality prediction and sequence design as an online tool or B) Generate a version of their code that runs in a free cloud-hosted service for scientific computing such as a Google Colaboratory, which would allows users to easily run their code with all necessary imports, including the data provided from the paper. This Google Colab notebook should run training and inference of their RBM architecture along with any comparison analytics and result generation, which the audience of nature comm would greatly appreciate. I understand this second option would require the authors to make an implementation of their source code using Python instead of Julia, which is why the first option may be a preferable path for the authors to improve their work. In my opinion, the second option would be easier to maintain and would allow readers to access a working version of this code with ease and without relying on the author's servers.
We believe that maintaining the codebase in Julia, instead of Python, facilitates reproducibility. Julia’s package manager automatically downloads and installs all necessary dependencies, with compatible versions, and is usually much more robust than Python’s dependency resolvers.
We have worked on the documentation of our package to facilitate local installation for new users. We simplified the setup and wrote simple instructions in the README.md page. We have also provided Jupyter notebooks (besides the Pluto notebooks), which might be more popular for some users.
We will also consider hosting a server in the future. However, due to the computational effort to train a RBM (requiring a few hours of compute on a standard CPU), we cannot offer such a service on-demand at the moment.
Lastly, we created a new Repository in Python: https://github.com/cossio/SamApp2024Py, that allows to train and sample RBM on RNA sequence families. This repository is now linked from our main repository, and should help users who prefer Python over Julia. We note that both Julia and Python notebooks can be executed in Google Colab, if remote execution is preferred (this also mentioned in our repository README now).
Beyond the previous comments, this work's methodology appears sound, and its main conclusions and claims seem to be justified, particularly through its experimental data with 476 RBM-designed sequences. As an experimentalist myself, I appreciate that and congratulate the authors for doing so.
We appreciate the comment, and thank Reviewer 1 for her/his efforts to assess our work.
